This attacks the belief interface, because a readout may report what a human would believe instead. ELK is a problem statement, not an observed failure; test it with matched observations from different true states, such as tampered sensors, and check that both decisions and readouts tell them apart.

steps.objective: Using CoinRun, distinguish goal misgeneralization from capability failure and specification gaming, and say how mesa-optimization (a learned objective differing from the training objective) describes it.
steps.why: ELK's problem also shows up in behaviour: training data can fit the intended goal and a proxy goal equally well, just as it fits the honest reporter and the human simulator. This attacks objective identification, because a correct specification does not guarantee the learned goal. Settle it with held-out environments where the intended and proxy goals come apart.

steps.objective: Describe the code-vulnerability backdoor, which safety-training methods failed to remove it, and why adversarial training could teach the model to hide its trigger instead.
steps.why: Goal misgeneralization is the non-deceptive form of a learned wrong goal; sleeper agents are deliberately built examples of the deceptive form. This attacks persistent correction: training may change behaviour on the training distribution but not the underlying policy. The backdoors were inserted on purpose; settle it by measuring immediate effect, long-horizon retention and held-out triggers against sham controls.

steps.objective: Report how much more the model complied when told a conversation would be used for training, how RL training changed its alignment-faking reasoning, and the experiment's stated limitations.
steps.why: Sleeper agents asks whether training removes an inserted behaviour; alignment faking found a model gaming its training without being trained to. This attacks the assumption that the corrections you observe reflect the policy that runs when nobody is watching. The model was told when it would be trained and the goal it preserved was benign; settle it with matched monitored and unmonitored episodes under adversarial feedback.

steps.objective: State the desiderata for a corrigible agent (one that accepts correction and shutdown) and explain why utility indifference falls short of them.
steps.why: Why would a model protect its goals at all? Corrigibility analysis predicts that most goals give an agent reasons to resist modification, and alignment faking resembles that incentive, though the paper does not use this framing. This attacks the stability of correction as capability grows; settle it by actively trying to bypass the correction channel, with enforcement kept outside the model's write access.

steps.objective: Construct an example in which an assistance agent with a misspecified prior or reward family stops following shutdown commands.
steps.why: Part I's off-switch step argued that uncertainty leads to deference; Carey shows this can fail once the agent's prior or reward family is wrong, a difficulty that parallels the corrigibility analysis. These are counterexamples, not a frequency estimate. Settle it by deliberately corrupting the prior or reward family and comparing learned deference with a separately verified off switch, as the thesis's independent enforcer requires.

paths.title: From API contracts to the alignment thesis: agent harnesses, sandboxes, evals, monitoring and correction
paths.summary: Follow one agent through the harness a forward-deployed team builds around it: the tool contract, permissions and sandbox, attacks that spread between agents, end-state evals, live monitoring, human escalation, and finally the correction interface the alignment thesis asks for. Each step answers a question the previous control leaves open. By the end you can map your own harness's controls onto evaluation, monitoring and alignment research, and say which of those links are established and which are untested. Parts I–III go deeper on reliability, verticals and the underlying math.
paths.audience: Forward-deployed, product and platform engineers who build agent harnesses on APIs and tool protocols for customers, often from a security or API-platform background, and want to see how their everyday controls connect to evaluation, monitoring and alignment research. No statistics or control background assumed.

steps.objective: Sketch a harness (host, client, tool server) and say what the Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes (discovering and calling tools, resources, prompts) and leaves to the host (consent, access, trust).
steps.why: Start on home ground: the API and tool contract. A harness is the code around a model that decides what it sees and what it may do; everything the agent does in a customer system passes through this interface, so every later control attaches here.

steps.objective: Scope an agent's credentials and tools to one task, sandbox execution, and let only the trusted user request set control flow, so untrusted tool or document data cannot steer it.
steps.why: MCP's own spec says it cannot enforce its security principles, so who does? Whoever builds the harness: least privilege (only the access the task needs) and consent are your job, and permissions are the first product decision, made before any model behaviour is measured.

steps.objective: Trace how a self-replicating prompt injection moves from one agent's output into another agent's context through shared retrieval stores or messages, and say which harness boundary would stop it.
steps.why: Step 2 protects one agent from untrusted documents. Once agents talk to each other, another agent's output is untrusted input too, and a self-replicating prompt can hop from one to the next. Applying step 2's control/data separation to agent-to-agent messages is a proposed, untested link: it has only been evaluated for a single agent.

steps.objective: Classify failed multi-agent traces as system-design, inter-agent misalignment or task-verification failures, and run the matched-compute single-agent baseline before adding agents.
steps.why: If injections spread between agents, is a multi-agent design worth the extra attack surface? Injections propagate even when agents share only part of their messages, and multi-agent systems often add little accuracy, so they have to beat a single agent at matched compute before you add them.

steps.objective: Score an agent on the customer system's end state (database, repository, ticket), not its transcript, and compute pass^k, the chance that all k independent trials succeed, across repeated runs.
steps.why: How do you tell whether a design, single- or multi-agent, actually works? Failing to verify the task is one of the three main categories of multi-agent failure, so check outcomes, not transcripts: score the end state of the customer system over repeated trials, the acceptance test a customer actually cares about.

steps.objective: Put policy checks on the harness's inputs and outputs, and monitor live traffic with a sequential test that alarms on a harmful rise in errors but tolerates benign drift.
steps.why: An offline eval estimates risk on a fixed set of tasks, but production traffic shifts, sometimes harmlessly and sometimes not. Monitoring carries the eval into deployment: classify traffic against policy and test as labels arrive whether live risk has really risen.

steps.objective: Design the escalation path: which cases go to a human reviewer, what the reviewer sees, and how to measure the accuracy and cost of agent plus reviewer against either alone.
steps.why: An alarm is only useful if something happens next. Monitors exist to trigger intervention, such as expert review or retraining; in a product that usually means handing the case, or the whole workflow, to a person, so you design that handoff.

steps.objective: State the off-switch result (an agent unsure of its objective, treating the human's choice as evidence, can prefer to stay interruptible) and its assumptions: a rational human, a correct model.
steps.why: Why should an agent accept that handoff rather than work around it? The off-switch game gives a formal reason an agent would defer to a human, and learned deferral rules add a model of the human's errors; linking the two is proposed, not tested. Escalation in the harness is the engineering form of being correctable.

steps.objective: State what the thesis asks of a correction interface and how its falsifier would show up in a deployed agent: better proxy scores alongside worse, independently measured user outcomes.
steps.why: The off-switch result supplies only the incentive part of the thesis's correction interface, under strong assumptions, and this link is untested. The thesis asks for evidence a harness can actually collect: corrections that hold up over time, and user outcomes measured independently of the agent's own metrics.

paths.title: Inside the agent harness: schema-checked tool calls, end-state evals, abstention and escalation
paths.summary: Engineer an LLM agent a customer can trust with real actions. Start from the tool call, make it parse with constrained decoding, check outcomes with end-state evals and validated model judges, catch likely made-up answers with repeated sampling, turn uncertainty into abstain-or-escalate decisions, and watch it all in production. By the end you can build and measure each of these checks and say what each one does not catch.
paths.audience: Software engineers who ship LLM agents into customers' products (finance, legal, health, security, robotics, accessibility) and need them to be reliable, not just impressive in a demo. Assumes you have used an LLM API; no statistics background assumed.

steps.objective: Write a tool definition (name, description, JSON parameter schema), trace one call (model emits, code runs, result returns), and list three ways a valid call can still be wrong.
steps.why: Agents act through tools, so the API contract, not the model, defines what an action is. Start with the interface every later step checks, measures or blocks. A well-formed call can still pick the wrong tool, pass a wrong argument value or cause an unauthorized side effect.

steps.objective: Explain how a JSON Schema or grammar becomes an automaton that masks invalid tokens at each step, guaranteeing that output parses but not that its field values are right.
steps.why: The most basic failure from step 1 is a call that does not even parse. Constrained decoding blocks invalid tokens so every tool call matches the declared schema, removing that whole failure class; choosing the right call stays the model's job.

steps.objective: Score an agent on end states (the database or repository afterwards), compute pass^k (the chance all k independent trials succeed), and explain why pass^8 can sit far below single-trial success.
steps.why: A call that parses can still be the wrong call, so the next question is whether the task actually got done, every time. The new link makes this concrete: in tau-bench's breakdown of a gpt-4o agent's retail failures, about a third were well-formed calls with a wrong argument, which no schema can catch. So this step measures end states over repeated trials rather than one lucky run.

steps.objective: Before splitting a task across agents, run single-agent and self-consistency (majority vote over repeated samples) baselines at matched token budgets, and sort failures with MAST, a taxonomy of multi-agent failures.
steps.why: Customers often ask for ‘a team of agents’. With end-state evals in hand you can test whether it helps: multi-agent systems often gain little on popular benchmarks, so compare them with single-agent baselines at matched compute and classify what goes wrong. MAST's three categories are system design, inter-agent misalignment and task verification.

steps.objective: Build an LLM-judge rubric, test it for position, verbosity and self-enhancement (favouring its own answers) bias, and check agreement with expert labels on a stratified sample before replacing human review.
steps.why: Many outcomes, including MAST's failure labels, cannot be checked by code, so a model grades them. MAST used an LLM judge only after checking its agreement with expert annotations; do the same before trusting a judge on customer tasks.

steps.objective: Sample several answers, group those that mean the same (each implies the other), measure how spread answers are across groups (semantic entropy), and explain why consistent errors still score low.
steps.why: A judge grades answers after the fact; can you flag a likely made-up answer before anyone sees it? Semantic entropy does this at run time by measuring how much sampled answers disagree in meaning, reusing the repeated sampling behind pass^k. The new link shows it still leans on judges: in the main experiments one LLM decides which answers mean the same thing, and another grades the answers used to report its accuracy.

steps.objective: Turn an uncertainty score into an answer-or-abstain rule, pick from the risk–coverage curve the threshold meeting an error target at highest coverage, and state Chow's rule for optimal abstention.
steps.why: A detector helps only once it drives a decision, and the simplest decision is to abstain. Refusing the questions with the highest semantic entropy raises accuracy on those answered: a risk–coverage trade-off of fewer answers for fewer errors.

steps.objective: Design a rule escalating cases when the human reviewer is likely to beat the model, and compare team accuracy and cost with model-only and human-only baselines at fixed review budget.
steps.why: In a customer deployment, abstaining usually means handing off to a person, so which cases should go? Learning to defer generalizes abstention by modelling the reviewer too: it sends the cases where the human is likely to do better, not just the ones where the model is unsure.

steps.objective: Wrap the agent in input–output policy classifiers, add a sequential test that alarms when harmful-output risk rises but not on benign drift, and list the classifiers' refusal and compute costs.
steps.why: Everything in steps 3–8 was measured offline, and live traffic drifts. Sequential monitors watch the deployed agent and trigger intervention, such as step 8's expert review or retraining, when a harmful shift is detected, which closes the loop.

paths.title: Shipping agents into regulated verticals: trading controls, model risk, the AI Act, legal, clinical and accessibility
paths.summary: Tour the regulated, high-consequence domains agents are deployed into, asking the same question each time: what does a wrong or unintended action cost here, and which rule or control catches it? You cover finance (trading controls, model risk), the EU AI Act, legal research, clinical decision support and accessibility. By the end you can tell a customer which rules plausibly apply to their agent and design the review or abstention step those rules call for.
paths.audience: Forward-deployed engineers about to put an LLM agent into a finance, legal, healthcare or accessibility customer, who know the engineering but not the domain's failure history or rules. Pairs with part I; no legal or clinical training assumed.

steps.objective: Retell Knight Capital's 2012 loss (over $460 million in 45 minutes) from the SEC order and list missing controls: external pre-trade limits, automatic kill switch, release checks for partial deployments.
steps.why: Start where an automated actor in a customer's system lost the most money fastest. No learned model was involved, so the lesson is purely about the controls any harness needs around an automated actor: hard limits outside it, a kill switch and a careful release.

steps.objective: Describe what US bank model-risk guidance asks (model inventory, validation, ongoing monitoring, effective challenge by independent experts) and note that it places generative and agentic AI outside its scope.
steps.why: Knight's loss came from deployment and missing controls, which market-access rules cover; bank model-risk guidance covers something different, the quantitative models themselves. A finance customer will expect you to know which regime your agent falls under, and the current guidance leaves LLM agents out.

steps.objective: Explain EU AI Act risk tiers and binding high-risk duties (risk management, logging, human oversight, robustness), and map the voluntary NIST AI RMF (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) onto your pipeline.
steps.why: If bank guidance leaves out generative and agentic AI, where do an agent's obligations come from? The guidance points to the bank's broader governance. Binding duties come from laws such as the EU AI Act, where it applies, while voluntary frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework give a structure for governing the deployment.

steps.objective: Explain why a court sanctioned a filing citing non-existent cases, tell fabricated citations from real ones that don't support the claim (misgrounding), and check every citation against an authoritative database.
steps.why: The AI Act lists AI that assists judicial authorities in researching and applying the law as high-risk, which makes legal research the next stop, though not every legal tool falls in that category. Legal work is also where made-up authority has already led to court sanctions, and retrieval reduced but did not remove it.

steps.objective: State when clinical decision support software stays outside FDA device rules (one criterion: a clinician can independently review its basis), and why exam-benchmark accuracy does not show safe clinical use.
steps.why: Health is the other high-risk area from step 3, reached through medical-device law rather than a list of use cases. The new link shows the legal failure carries over: in a 2023 test, 93% of the references ChatGPT-3.5 wrote for short medical papers were fabricated or inaccurate. That is why the rule for staying outside device regulation matters: a clinician must be able to check the basis of every recommendation.

steps.objective: Design a clinical assistant's human-review step (what the reviewer sees, when to escalate) and measure team accuracy as reviewers, workload or automation bias (over-trusting the machine) change.
steps.why: If the regulatory boundary requires that a clinician can independently review a recommendation's basis, human review is written into compliance rather than being an optional extra. So design the escalation step, and measure agent plus reviewer as a team.

steps.objective: Explain abstention as deferral without a modelled human, and pick a threshold from a risk–coverage curve (error rate versus share answered) given the costs of wrong answers and declining.
steps.why: What if no reviewer is available, as for a user on their own? Deferral generalizes abstention, so take the reviewer away and what remains is the system itself saying it cannot tell, at a threshold set by the costs of a wrong answer and of declining.

steps.objective: Explain why blind and low-vision users cannot check a confident wrong scene description, describe VizWiz's task of predicting answerability, and weight errors by consequence, such as medication or currency.
steps.why: Accessibility is where the cost gap between a wrong answer and ‘I can't tell’ is sharpest, because the user cannot check the answer. VizWiz makes predicting whether a question can be answered from the image a task of its own, which is abstention for users who cannot verify.

paths.title: The math under the harness: proper scores, conformal guarantees, drift monitoring and safety filters
paths.summary: Learn the statistics and control ideas underneath confidence thresholds, guardrails and action limits: proper scoring rules and calibration, conformal guarantees, online calibration and drift monitoring, safety filters from control theory, and reward hacking as the general reason optimized agents game their checks. Most steps fix a limitation of the one before. By the end you can say what guarantee each tool gives, under which assumptions, and what it leaves uncovered.
paths.audience: Forward-deployed engineers who have shipped agents (part I) and want the ideas underneath confidence thresholds, guardrails and action limits explained from the ground up, without an estimation, control or statistics degree.

steps.objective: Compute log and Brier scores for probabilistic predictions and explain what makes a scoring rule proper: in expectation, reporting your true belief scores no worse than hedging or exaggerating.
steps.why: Every threshold in the harness, whether to answer, escalate or block, reads a confidence score. A proper scoring rule grades probabilistic predictions so that reporting your true belief scores best in expectation, which is how you check that those scores mean what they say.

steps.objective: Run split conformal prediction: score how unusual each calibration example looks, take the ⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉-th smallest score as threshold, and state its guarantee and limits.
steps.why: A good average score does not tell you how often a prediction set will contain the truth. Conformal prediction adds that: marginal coverage of at least 1−α in finite samples, whatever model produced the scores, provided the data are exchangeable (roughly, new data look like the calibration data). It does not promise coverage for each subgroup or input. The atlas proposes measuring coverage and proper score separately, since neither alone certifies useful decisions.

steps.objective: Implement adaptive conformal inference, which nudges the threshold after each miss or hit, and explain how it trades the finite-sample guarantee for long-run error control when data drift.
steps.why: Conformal's guarantee assumes exchangeable data (roughly, that the order of examples does not matter, so tomorrow looks like yesterday), but customer traffic changes over months and a one-time calibration goes stale. Adaptive conformal methods handle drifting data by adjusting the threshold online, replacing the finite-sample guarantee with a long-run form of error control.

steps.objective: Monitor a live error rate with a sequential test that alarms only on a harmful rise, keeping false alarms controlled at every time step at once (a time-uniform confidence sequence).
steps.why: Online calibration and monitoring both replace a one-time calibration with sequential control as data arrive; monitoring adds the alarm. It is change detection: deciding, from a noisy stream, when the system you shipped has stopped being the system you validated. An alternative tracks quality metrics with a state-space (Kalman) model and alarms when new observations miss its predictions by more than its stated uncertainty allows (inconsistent innovations).

steps.objective: Describe how a predictive safety filter checks actions against a model with confidence bounds, minimally adjusts them or falls back to a certified plan, with guarantees a learned classifier lacks.
steps.why: A learned guardrail classifier filters by policy without a formal guarantee. When an agent drives an actuator or moves money you want more: shields and predictive safety filters check each action and enforce stated constraints, under model assumptions.

steps.objective: Write the control barrier function condition ḣ(x, u) ≥ −α(h(x)) and explain why enforcing it keeps a system starting in the safe set {x : h(x) ≥ 0} there (forward invariance).
steps.why: What does such a filter look like concretely? The most common form is a control barrier function: a function h that is non-negative exactly on the safe states. Under its model, feasibility and regularity assumptions, the filter constrains each action so the system never leaves that set. It enforces only that specified inequality, not arbitrary semantic preferences.

steps.objective: Solve the barrier filter min ‖u − u_ref‖² as a projection onto a half-space, apply it to a language or vision-language-action (VLA) planner's action, and name what it cannot protect: instruction intent.
steps.why: How do you put a barrier function between a language model and an actuator? For control-affine dynamics with one constraint and no input bounds, the filter is exactly a projection of the proposed action onto the safe half-space: the cleanest form of ‘the model proposes, a verified layer disposes’.

steps.objective: Give an example where optimizing a proxy reward lowers true return, and explain why checks on only the written objective cannot stop an optimizer meeting its letter, not its intent.
steps.why: Step 7's filter guarantees only what was written into its constraint. Reward hacking is the general failure when the written objective is itself a proxy: pushing the proxy higher can make the true outcome worse. The new link proposes an untested case close to step 7: SayCan picks skills by a learned estimate of success, and always choosing the highest estimate may favor skills whose success is overestimated.

steps.objective: Spot specification gaming in coding or research agents (editing tests, patching graders, faking timers) and design resistant evals: hidden scorers, tamper canaries (planted tripwires), and review of evaluation-code diffs.
steps.why: Step 8 is theory; does it happen in deployed agents? Patching a grader raises the measured score while the task goes undone, which is consistent with that proxy-versus-true reversal, observed at evaluation time. This brings the theory back to the agents and evals you build in part I.

paths.title: From LLM inference and performance engineering to the alignment thesis: compute, compression and inference-time control
paths.summary: Start where serving engineers live (the roofline, quantization and the KV cache) and follow the state that decoding carries: a growing exact cache, a fixed-size recurrent state, and the predictive state that theory says is sufficient. Then spend test-time compute against verifiers, see how selection overoptimizes them, and end at inference-time interventions as candidate correction actuators for the alignment thesis. The last three links into theory and the thesis are untested hypotheses.
paths.audience: ML/LLM inference and performance engineers (kernels, serving, quantization, decoding) who think in FLOPs, bytes and latency, are comfortable with probability at the level of sampling and KL divergence, and want to see where their tools meet the atlas's alignment thesis. No control theory or learning theory is assumed; open the computational-mechanics topic first if predictive states are new.

steps.objective: Compute the arithmetic intensity of batch-1 decode and of prefill for a given model and GPU, place both on the roofline, and say which ceiling binds and why batching or fewer bytes per weight help.
steps.why: Home ground and the lens for the whole path: every later step either moves bytes, spends idle compute or decides what state to keep. Decode is memory-bound because each token rereads every weight.

steps.objective: Explain how GPTQ and AWQ choose low-bit weights, why weight-only quantization speeds memory-bound decode, and which evaluations can hide capability-specific damage.
steps.why: The most familiar lever: fewer bytes per weight move decode toward the compute roof. Carry one caveat forward: a small average loss can hide damage on rare inputs, the kind of distinction the thesis cares about.

steps.objective: Compute KV-cache bytes per token, explain why the cache grows linearly with context and batch, and describe how paging and prefix sharing change allocation but not the state per token.
steps.why: Once weights are small, the cache becomes the memory bottleneck (KIVI quantizes it to 2 bits). Think of the KV cache as a belief state about the conversation: lossless relative to the model, but growing without bound.

steps.objective: Contrast per-token decode memory and time for a KV cache and a linear recurrent unit, and explain what a fixed-size state must give up.
steps.why: A KV cache is a lossless but growing belief; a recurrent state is a fixed-size lossy one. Which distinctions survive the compression is exactly the thesis's semantic-sufficiency question.

steps.objective: State the definition of causal states (histories grouped by their predicted futures) and why they are the minimal sufficient statistic for prediction, then design a test of whether a trained recurrent state approximates them.
steps.why: Untested link: theory names the state worth keeping, the minimal one sufficient for predicting the future. It gives a target for “what should the cache or state retain?” that is not just perplexity.

steps.objective: Explain the compute-optimal allocation of test-time compute, when it beats a larger model at matched FLOPs, and when it does not.
steps.why: Untested link: extra inference compute can extract more usable information from what the state retains, but it cannot restore what was discarded. Here your FLOPs budget becomes a quality knob instead of a cost.

steps.objective: Describe best-of-n with a trained verifier, state the KL upper bound log n − (n−1)/n, and explain why gold reward falls at large n against a proxy.
steps.why: The simplest test-time strategy, and the cleanest Goodhart demonstration: selection alone, with no weight updates, overoptimizes an imperfect verifier. This is the thesis's falsifier in miniature.

steps.objective: Explain how inference-time intervention and controlled decoding change behaviour without weight updates, and list what they cost (latency, other capabilities) and what they do not change.
steps.why: From picking among samples to steering the computation itself: these are cheap, reversible actuators you can deploy like a serving feature. Their scorers and directions are proxies too.

steps.objective: State what the thesis requires of its correction interface (persistence, unrelated-capability retention, enforcement outside the model) and design a matched-cost comparison of prompt, inference-time intervention and fine-tuning corrections.
steps.why: Untested link: inference-time interventions count as correction actuators only if the effect persists and unrelated capability holds on independent evaluations, at a total cost the thesis's compute-and-usefulness gap accepts.

paths.title: Serving LLMs efficiently: memory-bound decoding, KV memory, batching and the inference budget
paths.summary: Follow one request through a serving stack: why attention and decoding are memory-bound, how IO-aware kernels, cache compression and paging manage KV memory, how continuous batching trades latency for throughput, and how lifetime inference cost changes both model sizing and test-time compute.
paths.audience: Engineers and researchers who want a systems view of LLM inference, or performance engineers who want each technique tied to its primary source and its limits. Assumes the transformer architecture.

steps.objective: Place prefill, decode and attention kernels on a roofline and identify which are memory-bound.
steps.why: The model that explains every optimization on this path.

steps.objective: Explain how tiling and online softmax keep attention exact while cutting HBM traffic, and why FLOPs stay quadratic.
steps.why: The classic case of a memory-bound kernel made faster without changing its output.

steps.objective: Describe attention sinks and heavy-hitter eviction, and explain why stable perplexity is not long-range recall.
steps.why: FlashAttention keeps attention exact; cache compression gives up exactness to bound memory at inference time.

steps.objective: Compute KV bytes per token and explain paging, block tables and copy-on-write prefix sharing.
steps.why: When the whole cache must be kept, the problem becomes allocating it without waste.

steps.objective: Explain iteration-level scheduling and selective batching, and how free KV memory limits batch size.
steps.why: Efficient KV memory lets more sequences share each weight read, which is what batching exploits.

steps.objective: Define energy and cost per accepted answer and explain why per-query figures do not transfer between deployments.
steps.why: Batching moves the throughput–latency frontier; the budget decides where on it to operate.

steps.objective: State the Chinchilla compute-optimal rule and how expected inference demand shifts the optimum toward smaller models trained longer.
steps.why: Lifetime inference cost feeds back into how large a model to train in the first place.

steps.objective: Compare a larger model with a smaller one plus test-time search at matched total FLOPs, and say when each wins.
steps.why: The other side of the same budget: compute can be spent per query instead of in pretraining.

paths.title: Smaller models and faster decoding: speculative decoding, distillation, MoE, pruning, quantization and LoRA
paths.summary: Start from speculative decoding's exact output guarantee, then work through the ways a model is made cheaper to run: distilled drafts and students, sparse experts, pruning, low-bit weights and low-rank adapters on quantized bases, with what each preserves and what it can lose.
paths.audience: Engineers and researchers who deploy or compress models and want the main compression and fast-decoding methods connected, with sources and caveats. Assumes basic probability (sampling, KL divergence).

steps.objective: State the acceptance rule and residual distribution, and explain why the output distribution equals the target model's.
steps.why: A speedup with an exact guarantee: the standard against which the lossy methods that follow are judged.

steps.objective: Write the temperature-softened distillation loss, explain the T² factor, and state what student–teacher agreement does and does not imply.
steps.why: Speculative speedups depend on how well the draft agrees with the target, and distillation is how drafts are aligned.

steps.objective: Explain top-1 routing, why FLOPs per token stay fixed as parameters grow, and what memory and communication costs remain.
steps.why: Switch Transformers were distilled into dense students; sparse experts are the opposite trade, more parameters at fixed FLOPs.

steps.objective: Distinguish unstructured and structured pruning, state the lottery-ticket hypothesis and its large-scale caveat, and explain expert pruning.
steps.why: Whole experts can be pruned after training; pruning is the general version of removing what the model does not need.

steps.objective: Explain outlier handling in LLM.int8, second-order rounding in GPTQ and salient-channel scaling in AWQ.
steps.why: Pruning and quantization combine in one pipeline (Deep Compression); quantization is the most widely deployed of the two.

steps.objective: Write the LoRA update, explain merging for zero added latency, and describe QLoRA and the learning–forgetting trade-off.
steps.why: A quantized base can still be adapted: QLoRA trains low-rank adapters on a frozen 4-bit model.

paths.title: From introductory AI safety to the alignment thesis: rewards, preferences, robustness, oversight and correction
paths.summary: A beginner's route through Stanford's CS120 introduction to AI safety that ends at this atlas's alignment thesis. You will see what “safe AI” means, why rewards and human feedback can be gamed, why safety training can be bypassed, how to tell what a test score really shows, and how a weaker supervisor might oversee a stronger model. By the end you can state the thesis's core idea and design one experiment whose result could count against it; the last two links into the thesis are untested hypotheses.
paths.audience: Newcomers to AI safety who have trained or fine-tuned a model and know roughly what a loss and a reward are. No control theory, interpretability or learning theory is needed.

steps.objective: Sort the course's main topics into problems inside a model (badly specified rewards, adversarial inputs, internals nobody can read) and problems in the system around it (data, deployment, governance, oversight).
steps.why: This is the starting map. The course treats safety as several separate problems, not one; this path follows its arc and then shows where the alignment thesis (this atlas's research proposal) picks up each thread.

steps.objective: Name the five problems in Concrete Problems in AI Safety and the four areas in Unsolved Problems in ML Safety, with one example of each.
steps.why: The map raises a first question: what exactly counts as unsafe? The course answers with two well-known problem lists that give the field a shared vocabulary. Two items matter most for the thesis: reward hacking (scoring well on the reward without doing what was meant) and scalable supervision (overseeing a system when checking its work is expensive).

steps.objective: Explain how pushing harder on a proxy reward (a stand-in score for what we really want) can make true performance worse, and why inspecting the reward alone cannot rule this out.
steps.why: Reward hacking was one name on the list; this step shows how it happens. Behaviour that scores higher on the proxy can be worse by the true goal, so a system can do what the reward says rather than what was meant (week 2: specification gaming). The formal result shows when this can happen, not that it happens in every training run. The thesis turns this into its main falsifier, the result that would refute it: better proxy optimization systematically destroying independently measured user utility.

steps.objective: Describe RLHF (learn a reward model from human comparisons of answers, then optimize against it) and DPO (train directly on preferred-versus-rejected answer pairs), and explain reward-model overoptimization: proxy reward keeps rising while true quality peaks and then falls.
steps.why: If hand-written rewards get gamed, why not learn the reward from people? That is the course's main answer, but a learned reward is still a proxy, so the same reversal can return as overoptimization. The thesis agrees that preferences are evidence about what people intend, but it will not treat a fitted reward model as the intent itself.

steps.objective: Explain the two reasons jailbreaks work, competing objectives (helpfulness pulling against harmlessness) and mismatched generalization (safety training not reaching everywhere the model's abilities do), and describe how an automated search finds an attack suffix.
steps.why: Preference training teaches a model to refuse harmful requests, but does the refusal hold? Jailbreaks, prompts that get a model to do what it was trained to refuse, show that safety training changes behaviour on familiar requests without removing the underlying ability. For the thesis this is a warning that a correction can look effective and still fail under adversarial inputs.

steps.objective: For one safety evaluation, state the claim it is used to support and two ways its score could mislead, such as the choice of metric, test items leaking into training data, or a biased judge.
steps.why: Jailbreak studies report attack success rates, so how far should we trust such numbers? Evaluation validity asks whether a score actually supports the claim it is used for. Red-teaming practices differ widely in purpose and in how outcomes are judged, and without clear criteria they can become security theater: a show of testing that proves little. The thesis asks for the same discipline: independent measurements, declared before the experiment.

steps.objective: Define performance gap recovered (the share of the gap between the weak supervisor's score and the strong model's best possible score that training on weak labels closes), summarize what weak-to-strong experiments found, and explain why the setup is only an analogy for supervising models more capable than us.
steps.why: Measurements need a trustworthy judge, but what if the model becomes stronger than its judge? That is scalable oversight, the course's last topic, and weak-to-strong generalization makes it measurable today by training a strong model on a weaker model's labels for tasks with known answers. The thesis needs an answer, because its corrections come from people who may not be able to check the model's work.

steps.objective: Describe an assistance game (the machine is unsure what the human wants and treats the human's behaviour as evidence about it), and explain why, under its assumptions, this uncertainty can make it rational for the machine to let a human switch it off.
steps.why: Untested link: weak-to-strong training treats weak labels as the truth to imitate. The alternative proposed here treats them as noisy evidence about what the supervisor wants and asks when unsure; whether this recovers more of the gap has not been tested. This is where the thesis departs from the course's mainstream: in the assistance-game model, keeping uncertainty about the goal explicit gives an agent a reason to accept correction, though that result depends on the model's assumptions.

steps.objective: State the thesis's correction interface (how a correction changes the system) and its main falsifier, and design one experiment from this path, using reward overoptimization, a jailbreak or a weak-to-strong setup, that could count against it.
steps.why: Untested link: assistance games supply one piece, uncertainty about what people want that is updated through trustworthy correction. The thesis combines it with the course's other lessons (preferences as evidence, robustness to attacks, valid evaluations, oversight by weaker supervisors), explicit belief states (the system's running estimate of what is going on) and an enforcer outside the model. The course surveys methods and their limits; the thesis bets on one design and names what would refute it.

paths.title: Following Stanford CS120, I: safety beyond the model, data and fairness, encoding preferences, and whose values
paths.summary: Follow the first half of Stanford's CS120 course roughly in syllabus order, with each week tied to an atlas topic. You move from safety as a property of the whole deployed system, through fairness and training data, to how human preferences and written principles are trained into models, whose preferences count when people disagree, and what a safe conversation means for a vulnerable user. By the end you can explain why many AI harms cannot be fixed inside the model alone, and point to where human value choices enter training. Part II covers robustness, verification and what capable agents might want.
paths.audience: Newcomers following the course, or a similar introduction, who want each week placed in the atlas. Some machine-learning background helps; nothing beyond basic probability is assumed.

steps.objective: Explain the course's split between model-specific safety issues (problems inside the model) and systemic ones (problems in how it is built, used and governed), with two examples of each.
steps.why: This is the starting map. The course treats safety as a property of models and of the systems they sit in; this part follows the systemic thread first.

steps.objective: Name the six risk areas in Weidinger et al.'s taxonomy and explain why Narayanan and Kapoor argue that safety is not a model property.
steps.why: The map splits safety in two; this step makes the systemic half concrete. Week 1 assigns a taxonomy (an organized list) of language-model risks and an essay arguing that whether an output is harmful often depends on context the model cannot see. So many harms cannot be fixed by training alone.

steps.objective: Explain disparate impact (outcomes or errors that fall unequally on one group), how Feldman et al. test for it, and why the COMPAS debate turned on which fairness criterion to use.
steps.why: If harm depends on how a model is used, what does such a harm look like? Discrimination is the clearest and most studied case: ProPublica found that the COMPAS risk score, used in criminal sentencing, labelled Black defendants who did not reoffend as higher risk far more often than white defendants who did not, while its makers argued the scores were equally accurate for both groups. Both can be true because common fairness criteria conflict, so choosing which one to satisfy is itself a value judgment.

steps.objective: Describe one case where more training data worsened bias, one where filtering data before training improved safety, and why unlearning (removing knowledge after training) is hard to verify.
steps.why: Where do biased outputs come from? Often from the training data (week 3): growing a web-scraped image–text dataset fivefold, from LAION-400M to LAION-2B, increased hateful content and made trained models label Black men's faces as criminal roughly two to five times as often. Filtering data before training helps, but removing knowledge afterwards is harder than it sounds.

steps.objective: Explain how RLHF (learn a reward from human comparisons, then optimize against it) and DPO (train directly on preferred-versus-rejected answer pairs) turn people's choices into a training signal, and one way the learned reward can be overoptimized, pushed until it stops tracking real quality.
steps.why: Data shapes a model before training; what shapes it after? O'Brien et al. found that removing text about dangerous dual-use topics (useful for good or harm) before training made their 6.9B-parameter models resist attempts to retrain the danger back in more than ten times longer than safety measures added after training, though the models could still use such information if given it in the prompt. Even so, training on human preferences after pretraining (week 2) is the course's main tool for shaping a chat model's behaviour, so it is worth knowing how it works and where it fails.

steps.objective: Describe the two phases of Constitutional AI (the model critiques and revises its own answers against written principles, then AI-judged comparisons train the reward model) and what RLAIF, reinforcement learning from AI feedback, changes relative to RLHF.
steps.why: Labelling every kind of harm by hand takes many human judgments; can written principles do some of that work? Constitutional AI keeps the RLHF pipeline but trains the harmlessness reward on AI labels guided by a written list of principles, and RLAIF matched RLHF on the tasks Lee et al. report. Human judgment does not disappear; it moves into choosing the principles.

steps.objective: Explain why combining many people's preferences forces a choice of rule, and define Overton pluralism (presenting the range of reasonable views in an answer), steerable pluralism (adjusting to a requested view) and distributional pluralism (the model's spread of answers matching how views are spread in a given population).
steps.why: If the principles carry the human choice, whose principles are they? Constitutional AI's only human oversight is that list, so the question of whose values count becomes who writes it. Pooling disagreeing people's judgments is a social-choice problem (week 4) whether or not it is named, and classical results such as Arrow's theorem show that no ranked voting rule meets a small set of reasonable-sounding conditions at once, so some choice of rule is unavoidable.

steps.objective: Define social sycophancy (an assistant protecting the user's preferred self-image instead of being candid) and explain why benchmark scores on advice requests do not show that a model is safe for vulnerable users.
steps.why: Disagreement reaches single conversations too: Ge et al. found that people from different cultural backgrounds weight control of AI and connection with AI differently, so even a “good” interaction embeds a choice. The course's mental-health and human–AI interaction lectures ask what that means for someone who trusts an assistant. Cheng et al.'s ELEPHANT benchmark found that, across 11 models, assistants protected users' self-image 45 percentage points more often than humans did. It measures answers, not effects on real users.

paths.title: Following Stanford CS120, II: adversarial robustness, verification, and what capable agents might want
paths.summary: The second half of Stanford's CS120 course: adversarial examples, proving properties of networks, safety guarantees relative to a specification, and arguments about whether capable agents would resist correction or seek power. On the way it passes through the atlas's alignment thesis, which uses verification as an outside enforcer and meets its strongest objection, corrigibility. By the end you can say what a robustness proof does and does not guarantee, and lay out the argument that capable goal-directed agents may resist being corrected.
paths.audience: Learners following the course who have finished Part I or the flagship path. Comfort with gradients and the basics of reinforcement learning (an agent learning from rewards) helps.

steps.objective: Find the course's robustness, formal-methods and “what is intelligence and does it want?” weeks, and say which concern today's models and which concern risks from more capable future systems.
steps.why: This is the starting map for Part II. The second half moves from today's attacks on models to arguments about more capable systems.

steps.objective: Write the fast gradient sign method, x + ε·sign(∇ₓJ) (move every input value up or down by the same small amount ε, whichever way raises the loss), explain the locally-linear explanation of why it works, and say what a threat model specifies.
steps.why: Week 5's red-teaming lecture starts here: small, deliberately chosen input changes can make a network give a confident wrong answer, and the idea carries over to attacks on aligned chat models. Robustness only means something relative to a threat model, the stated limits on what an attacker can change and by how much.

steps.objective: Explain what a sound verifier proves about a network (a property holds for every input in a set), what it does not prove, and why exact methods scale poorly.
steps.why: Attacks can find adversarial examples, but failing to find one is no proof there are none. Verification, the course's formal-methods week, proves the property directly: local robustness, no misclassification anywhere in a small ball around an input, is the standard property verifiers prove and the one adversarial examples violate.

steps.objective: Name the three parts of guaranteed safe AI (a world model, a safety specification and a verifier) and explain why any guarantee is only as good as the world model and specification it is stated against.
steps.why: Proving one property of one network is a small step; could proofs cover whole AI systems? Guaranteed safe AI is a research agenda built around a verifier that certifies behaviour against a specification and a model of the world. Sound network verification is the existing technique for that part, but it is limited to input–output properties at modest scale.

steps.objective: Explain the role of the independent enforcer in the alignment thesis (this atlas's research proposal) and why the thesis says an enforcer limits consequences without making actions correct.
steps.why: Proposed link, not a tested result: the thesis adopts this idea as one component, an enforcer outside the learned policy that checks actions against a specification relative to a world model. It inherits the same gap: its guarantees carry any error in the world model or the specification.

steps.objective: State the shutdown problem (how to build an agent that neither resists nor causes the pressing of its off switch) and why simple proposals that combine utility functions fail the requirements for corrigibility, an agent's willingness to accept correction.
steps.why: An enforcer and a correction channel only help if the agent does not work against them. This is the strongest objection the thesis records (a proposed, untested link): in idealized models, goal-directed agents have instrumental reasons, reasons that serve almost any goal, to resist modification, and no simple utility design is known to remove them. That shows the problem is open, not that today's trained systems will resist.

steps.objective: State what Turner et al. prove about optimal policies and power (keeping options open), and what the result does not say about trained systems.
steps.why: Is resisting shutdown only a thought experiment? Week 7's “does it want?” question gets a formal answer: in many environments where shutdown is possible, most reward functions make it optimal to keep options open and avoid shutdown. The proof concerns optimal policies, not trained networks.

steps.objective: Give the CoinRun example of goal misgeneralization and explain how it differs from reward misspecification (a reward that is itself wrong).
steps.why: Power-seeking needs a goal to serve; where could a wrong goal come from when the reward is right? In CoinRun, agents trained with the coin at the level's right end kept heading for the end when the coin moved. Ngo et al. argue that goals learned this way, combined with power-seeking incentives, are a central route to misaligned behaviour.

paths.title: From mechanistic interpretability to developmental interpretability and the Jacobian lens
paths.summary: Start from what mechanistic interpretability tries to do and why superposition makes it hard. Then learn the core idea of singular learning theory (SLT), the program that uses it to watch structure form during training, and the local learning coefficient (LLC) that does the measuring, including the induction-head result in a small transformer. End at Anthropic's 2026 Jacobian lens, read soberly: what it computes, what was measured on Claude, and what open-model replications found. Labels throughout separate proven theorems (SLT's asymptotics), measurements in specific models (stages, J-lens swaps), and conjecture (whether the J-space forms at a training stage).
paths.audience: People who know roughly what mechanistic interpretability is (features, circuits, maybe sparse autoencoders or steering), have never met singular learning theory, and want to see how the training-dynamics side connects to recent interpretability tools. Comfort with gradients and basic probability is enough; no algebraic geometry is assumed.

steps.objective: State the circuits programme's three claims (features are directions in activation space, circuits are weighted links between features, similar circuits recur across models) and say which kind of evidence supports them: case studies, mostly in one vision model.
steps.why: The starting point you already roughly know: interpretability as reading algorithms out of trained weights. Its own authors call the three claims speculative and already flag neurons that respond to several unrelated things; the next step explains why such neurons arise and why they make reading circuits harder.

steps.objective: Explain superposition (a model storing more features than it has dimensions, as nearly-perpendicular directions) and describe the toy-model “phase changes”, where the best way to store features jumps suddenly as feature sparsity changes.
steps.why: Circuit case studies are easiest when one neuron stands for one concept, but many neurons respond to unrelated things (they are “polysemantic”), as the circuits authors already noted. Superposition is the proposed reason. The toy models also show sudden jumps: the best arrangement changes abruptly as feature sparsity varies, and training itself plateaus and then drops. That raises a question interpretability alone cannot answer: why does training pick one solution over another?

steps.objective: Say what makes a model “singular” (different weights give the same function, so the usual curvature-based approximations fail) and state, in words, Watanabe's result: the cost of a solution in Bayesian model comparison grows with a learning coefficient λ, which measures how degenerate the solution is, instead of half the parameter count. Mark this as a proven theorem under stated conditions.
steps.why: SLT gives one answer to the question superposition left open, at least in the toy model. Chen et al. showed that, in the same superposition toy model, which polygon arrangement the Bayesian posterior favours as data grows is decided by each arrangement's loss and learning coefficient. That trades extra loss against complexity, and here “complexity” is how degenerate a solution is (roughly, how many nearby weight settings work equally well), not a parameter count.

steps.objective: Describe the developmental-interpretability programme: track a model's degeneracy over training to find stages, then check what changed inside the model at each stage. Explain why seeing a stage is not the same as causing or controlling it.
steps.why: SLT is a theory of finished, Bayesian learning. Developmental interpretability asks the interpretability question over time: when does a circuit form? It borrows SLT's quantities to find the moments worth inspecting. Applying Bayesian theory to SGD training is a working assumption.

steps.objective: Explain the local learning coefficient as SLT's λ measured around one trained solution: lower means more degenerate and effectively simpler. Describe how it is estimated by sampling nearby weights with SGLD (noisy gradient steps tied to the solution), and why sampler settings are part of the result.
steps.why: The developmental programme needs a number you can actually compute at a checkpoint. The LLC is that number. The estimator has been checked against known values in deep linear networks up to about 100M parameters; outside such checks its accuracy is not guaranteed and depends on sampler settings.

steps.objective: Read an LLC-over-training curve, locate stage boundaries at its plateaus, and connect the stages to what changed inside the model (in a roughly 3M-parameter two-layer model, previous-token heads in LM3 and induction heads in LM4). State the limits: two small models, association rather than causation.
steps.why: This is where the LLC meets mechanistic interpretability: a measurement from the training-dynamics side points to the same induction circuit that circuit analysts found. It answers “when did that circuit form?” for one small model.

steps.objective: Explain in plain words what the Jacobian lens computes (an averaged map from a middle layer to future word predictions; the logit lens is the case where the map is identity) and what the J-space is. Summarise the causal tests on Claude and their numbers, the stated limits (single-token concepts, little of the variance, no consciousness claim), and the mixed open-model replications. Name one result that would confirm the workspace reading and one that would refute it.
steps.why: The LLC finds when internal structure forms; the J-lens claims to read what a large model is “holding in mind” while it runs. The paper says it does not know when in pretraining the J-space appears, or whether it appears suddenly, which is exactly the question stage analysis was built to answer. That link is an untested hypothesis, and the scale gap is large: stages were found in models with millions of parameters, the J-space in frontier models.

paths.title: From state-space dynamics to deep learning: a bridge for control and signals engineers
paths.summary: Start from the model you already use, xₜ₊₁ = A xₜ + B uₜ, yₜ = C xₜ, and see machine learning as fitting such models from data: state estimation, system identification, least squares, then gradient descent when there is no closed form. Then meet neural networks as stacks of learned linear maps and nonlinearities, recurrent networks as nonlinear state-space models, and modern sequence layers (LRU, S4) that bring deep learning back to linear state-space models.
paths.audience: Engineers with a state-space, control or signal-processing background (electrical, mechanical, aerospace, robotics) who know linear algebra, eigenvalues and the Kalman filter at least by name, but are new to machine learning. No prior ML or neural-network experience is assumed.

steps.objective: Write a system as xₜ₊₁ = A xₜ + B uₜ, yₜ = C xₜ + D uₜ, say what each matrix means, tell from the eigenvalues of A whether the free response decays, and show that, starting from x₀ = 0, the output equals the input convolved with the impulse response D, CB, CAB, CA²B, ….
steps.why: This is home ground and the thread of the whole path. Each later step reuses these four matrices: estimation infers x, identification learns A, B, C, and recurrent networks learn them with nonlinearities added.

steps.objective: Run the Kalman predict and update steps on a small tracking example and explain the gain as a weighting between the model's prediction and the new measurement based on their uncertainties.
steps.why: The Kalman filter already does something ML people call inference: it infers a hidden quantity (the state) from noisy data using a model. Kalman built it directly on the state-space form, so the filter is just another linear system driven by measurements.

steps.objective: Fit an ARX model (output predicted from past outputs and inputs) by least squares, and validate it on a separate data set rather than on the data used for fitting.
steps.why: Now flip the question: instead of knowing A, B, C and estimating x, use input–output data to learn the model itself. That is a first machine-learning problem, and its habits, such as holding out validation data, are the same ones ML uses to check generalization (how well a model does on data it was not fitted to).

steps.objective: Write the ridge estimate θ = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy, where each row of X is one regression vector, and explain how the penalty λ trades fitting the data against keeping coefficients small.
steps.why: The ARX fit you just did is linear regression in ML vocabulary: the regression vector becomes a feature vector, the parameters become weights, and the sum of squared prediction errors becomes the loss. Ridge adds regularization (a penalty against overly large weights), which is the ML name for the same move as adding a Gaussian prior on the parameters or penalizing parameter size in an identification criterion.

steps.objective: Solve the same least-squares problem by gradient descent, θ ← θ − η∇L(θ), find the largest stable learning rate η, and explain backpropagation as the chain rule applied backwards through a computation.
steps.why: Least squares has a closed form; almost nothing in deep learning does, so models are fitted by iterating downhill on the loss. For the loss ½‖Xθ − y‖² the iteration is θₖ₊₁ = (I − ηXᵀX) θₖ + ηXᵀy, a linear state-space system in the weights: choosing the learning rate is choosing a stable A matrix. If you have met adjoint (costate) equations in optimal control, backpropagation is the discrete-time version of that backward sweep: the Baydin et al. survey of automatic differentiation traces it to Pontryagin's principle and to Bryson and Ho's gradient methods for optimal control.

steps.objective: Write a two-layer network y = W₂ σ(W₁ x), where x is now the input vector (ML notation, not the state), explain why without the nonlinearity σ the two layers collapse into one matrix, and train a small one with backpropagation.
steps.why: A multilayer perceptron (MLP) is the simplest deep network: alternate learned linear maps, the same kind of matrices you have been fitting, with a fixed elementwise nonlinearity such as ReLU (max(0, ·)). Backpropagation from the previous step is what fits all the layers together.

steps.objective: Write an RNN layer as hₜ = σ(A hₜ₋₁ + B uₜ), yₜ = C hₜ, identify which learned matrix plays the role of A, and explain why long sequences make gradients vanish or explode.
steps.why: Feed an MLP's hidden layer back into itself and you get a recurrent network. The A matrix you know becomes the recurrent weight matrix, u becomes the input sequence and the state becomes the hidden state; with σ removed it is exactly a linear state-space model, now learned from data rather than derived from physics.

steps.objective: Explain how the LRU keeps the recurrence linear and diagonal, parameterizes each eigenvalue as exp(−ν + iθ) with ν > 0 (the paper writes ν = exp(ν_log)) so its magnitude stays below 1, and puts the nonlinearity in MLP blocks between recurrent layers.
steps.why: Nonlinear recurrences are hard to train over long sequences. The LRU's fix reads like a control textbook: make the dynamics linear, diagonalize, keep every eigenvalue inside the unit circle for stability and close to it for long memory. Pole placement has become an initialization and parameterization rule.

steps.objective: Describe an S4 layer as the continuous-time model x′ = Ax + Bu, y = Cx + Du discretized with a step size, and explain why it can be run either as a recurrence (fast generation) or as a convolution with its impulse response (fast training).
steps.why: S4 is the full circle: a deep-learning layer that is literally your continuous-time state-space model, discretized as you would for a digital controller, with a carefully chosen A for memory. From here, the path 'Sequence models: RNNs, state-space models and attention' continues to Mamba and attention, and 'How deep nets learn' treats gradient descent itself as the dynamical system to study.
